Featured philosophy paper

Borrowed Integration

Aristotle on self-love, complete friendship, and what the experience of loss can reveal about a self that was never fully integrated on its own.

Thomas Nicol · Academic paper

It has been a few weeks since they left. I cannot sit in my apartment without something on. A podcast while I shower. A YouTube video while I eat. The constant hum of a playlist that I am not really listening to. The quiet is not exactly painful. It is more that I cannot find anything to do in it. I used to make the coffee just the way they liked it, each morning a quiet ritual of solidarity. We would sit at the counter and let the truth of our lives spill out between us. Now I drink my coffee alone, lit by the artificial glow of my phone, or among strangers in a quiet coffee shop where at least I can feel alone with others. They are gone and I miss them, but that is not what surprises me. What I did not expect is the restlessness, the way I cannot rest inside any room, any task, any version of myself that is not already half elsewhere. The absence is not where they used to be. It is in me. In all the small places I had not noticed they were holding up, and now that I see them, I cannot tell which were ever fully mine.

The standard way to read this kind of experience is as a measure of how much the person mattered. The bigger the hole, the deeper the love. I think that this reading misses something. Aristotle, read carefully, gives us a more uncomfortable explanation of why the loss hurts the way it does. In Nicomachean Ethics IX.4, Aristotle argues that the features of friendship are derived from a person's relation to themselves, meaning one must already be a friend to oneself before one can be a friend to another in the complete sense. He also describes, in the same chapter, what failed self-relation looks like from the inside: a person who cannot bear their own company and ends up fleeing into distraction.

When loss produces this specific kind of emptiness, the inability to occupy one's own solitude suggests the friendship the agent believed was complete was actually masking incompleteness on their side, and the friend's presence was supplying what they had not built themselves. The intensity of this devastation is then partly a measure of what they had outsourced. I will develop this idea in two steps: first the framework, Aristotle's account of self-love as the precondition of friendship, and the absence of self-love as what disguises a lower form of friendship as the highest kind. Then a return to the apartment, where the framework can tell us what the agent's pain is actually pointing at.

The pain reveals that the wholeness they felt during the relationship had been made possible partly by the friend rather than by themselves, and what remains is the divided soul they had never fully integrated on their own. According to Aristotle no agent would choose to be alone, as due to the nature of humans as political animals part of the natural good is spending time with others (NE IX.9, 1169b17-23). This establishes friendship as a necessary aspect of life. But what exactly is friendship? Aristotle gives us a concrete definition that I will build off of for the remainder of this argument. Aristotle defines complete friendship as a relationship in which each party wishes good to the other for the other's own sake, grounded in a mutual recognition of virtue (NE VIII.3, 1156b7-12). Crucially, he argues that this orientation toward another is not primary but derived, as the features of friendship proceed from a person's prior relation to themselves (NE IX.4, 1166a1-2). To be a complete friend to another is to extend toward an outside agent the same care, attention, and goodwill the virtuous person already directs toward their own rational self. Aristotle's definition of complete friendship establishes a clear precondition of self-integration. Without it, what looks and feels like friendship takes the shape of one of the two lower forms. Aristotle grounded these relationships, friendships of utility and friendships of pleasure, not in the other's own good but in what they provide. To understand why this matters for the agent in the apartment, we need to first understand what distinguishes these lower forms from a complete friendship.

Aristotle divides friendship into three distinct categories based on where the desire for the other moral agent comes from. The first of these is friendship of utility, the love built on a desire to use the other agent as the catalyst for one’s own personal growth. The second is friendship of pleasure, the act of loving someone because they are pleasant to be around. These are seen as incomplete forms of friendship, as when the utility ends or the pleasure fades the relationship has nothing remaining to stand on (NE VIII.3, 1156a10-24). The third kind is friendship in its fullest sense, where each party loves the other for who they are rather than for what they provide. The distinction matters because complete friendship has a structural precondition that the lower forms do not, being that each party must already be a friend to themselves. A relationship can look like complete friendship from the inside, can feel like it for years, and still fail to meet the standard if one or both parties have not done the prior work of self-integration. The question, then, is whether what looked like complete friendship from the inside actually was one.

The features of integrated self-relation all depend on the soul being unified, and the unintegrated person hardly has these features at all because their soul is divided against itself (NE IX.4, 1166b1-12). The virtuous person wishes themselves to exist and continue, wishes good for themselves, finds it pleasant to spend time alone with their own thoughts, and feels their joys and griefs as a single unified self rather than as a soul divided against itself (NE IX.4, 1166a18-29). Complete friendship is the extension of the same virtuous state toward another rational being who has done the same work of self-integration. Complete friendship cannot create self-integration; it can only extend it. The virtuous person's already-integrated self-relation is what is given to the friend, which means the friendship does not supply that integration, it presupposes it. The agent who has not done that prior work cannot, on Aristotle's account, give what they have not built.

What the absence of this work looks like, on Aristotle's account, is a person at war with themselves. The rational part of them deliberates and judges in one direction while desire pulls them in another. The agent knows what they should be and knows what they want but based on their character they find themselves engaging in the opposite actions. Because reason and desire are not pointed at the same thing, there is no coherent self for self-love to land on (NE IX.4, 1166b15-19). They are full of regret about past actions because the part of them that made the choice is not the part that now stands in judgment of it. They cannot grieve or rejoice as a unified self because the parts of their soul respond differently to the same event, with one part rejoicing while another part regrets, or one part grieving while another resents the grief (NE IX.4, 1166b20-26). The result is that being alone with their thoughts becomes intolerable, not because their interior is merely unpleasant but because it is structurally fragmented. There is no unified person to keep company with. So they flee themselves and seek the company of others, not as an extension of integrated selfhood but as an escape from a self they have not yet unified on their own.

Let us return now to the apartment. What appears in the agent's restlessness is not generic grief. It is the specific phenomenology Aristotle attributes to the soul divided against itself, the one that cannot stand its own company and seeks the company of others to escape. The agent says the quiet is not exactly painful, but they cannot find anything to do in the quiet, which is exactly the condition Aristotle describes when he says the unintegrated soul has no coherent concept of self to take pleasure in. This leaves the agent to flee into the company of others through social media, surrounding themselves with others, just as Aristotle says the unintegrated soul does. The agent uses others not as an extension of a unified self into a shared activity but rather as an escape from a self that has not been unified. Likewise, the restlessness the agent describes is what a divided soul produces when the pieces are no longer being supported by external stimuli. This is what the agent is pointing at when they say the missing is not where the friend used to be, but in them, in all the places they did not realize the friend was holding up.

The agent is not just sad. They are in the condition Aristotle described as the unintegrated soul, the one whose parts pull against each other and whose interior cannot be occupied alone. The natural first thought is that the loss itself produced this, that the friend’s leaving fractured a self that had been whole. But this is not what Aristotle’s framework describes. Self-integration on his account is the rational self being continuous and in agreement with itself. That condition is not the kind of thing another person's departure can remove. If the agent’s interior had been unified before the loss, the loss would have produced grief, but grief that still permits being alone with oneself. The fact that the loss has produced fragmentation rather than just sadness suggests that the unification was not the agent's to begin with. Rather, it was being supplied by their significant other.

Complete friendship, in the Aristotelian sense, requires self-integration on both sides, because friendship extends a unified self towards another rather than creating one. The agent’s current state of sorrow alludes to the notion that they did not have the integration that complete friendship presupposes. This means that the relationship they believed was the highest kind cannot have been complete in Aristotle’s sense. Instead, it was structurally one of the lower forms. The friend was loved in part for what they provided, and what they provided was not money or favors but something more disguised. They made the agent feel as though their own self was already whole. The love was real, but it was a love that depended on the friend's presence to keep the agent's own interior together. This is why the loss is not only the absence of someone the agent cared about, but also the collapse of a self they had not realized was being held up.

Aristotle himself says even the fully virtuous person needs friends and will suffer when those friends are lost (NE IX.9, 1169b16-22). If grief over a lost friend reveals incomplete self-integration, this reading seems to apply to everyone, including the people Aristotle holds up as the model of integrated selfhood. The reading does not pick out grief in general, though. It picks out a specific shape of grief. The virtuous person who loses a friend loses real shared activity, real shared discourse, particular things that could only be done with this person. They suffer, and Aristotle does not ask them not to. What they retain is the capacity to be alone with themselves. The agent in the apartment does not maintain this capacity. Grief that still permits solitude is the appropriate response to losing shared goods. Grief that makes solitude unbearable is the revelation of borrowed integration.

The uncomfortable consequence of this reading of Aristotle is that some of the pain felt is the collapse of the self-integration the agent had outsourced. The lonesomeness felt in the apartment is not only the absence of someone the agent cared about, it is the exposure of a self that had been incomplete the entire time, held together by a presence that has now withdrawn. The friendship was genuine in its affection and in its care, but it could not have been complete in Aristotle's strict sense because the agent had not yet built the self that complete friendship presupposes. The love was real, and the grief is real. Neither of these things is being questioned here. But the specific form of the pain, the inability to be alone with oneself, serves a greater purpose than mourning. It is pointing at something the friendship had been covering. The restlessness, the flight into background noise, is not just grief. It is a signal that something prior to the friendship was never fully the agent's own.
